summary: Documents how some requirements of RFC 1264, for advancing routing protocols to Draft Standard, have been met by LDP, specifically operational experience. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card that shows a protocol has worked well in real use.

subtitle: Report on how Label Distribution Protocol has performed in operational networks.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed to evaluate whether LDP was ready to advance from Proposed to Draft Standard status, requiring documented operational experience from real deployments.
tldr.mechanism: A survey was sent to network operators who had deployed LDP in their networks, requesting information about their environments, applications, protocol features, interoperability experience, and operational issues encountered.
tldr.outcome: Operators reported stable implementations with good scalability and few interoperability issues, supporting LDP's advancement through the standards process, though some protocol-level improvements were identified.

today: RFC 5037 documents operational experience that supported LDP's advancement to Draft Standard. The protocol is now specified in RFC 5036 and remains in use for MPLS label distribution in networks that do not require traffic engineering.

sections.title: The Standards Advancement Question
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) was published as RFC 3036 in January 2001 and later became RFC 5036. Before a protocol can advance from Proposed to Draft Standard status in the IETF standards track, it must demonstrate operational maturity through documented experience in real deployments. RFC 1264 defines the criteria for advancement, including a requirement for operational experience reports.

This RFC documents how operators answered a survey about their LDP deployments, providing the evidence needed for standards advancement. The survey was sent to the MPLS Working Group in October 2004 and received 11 responses from operators worldwide.
sections.plainLanguage: The standards body wanted to know if a routing protocol was mature enough to move up a level. They asked operators who were using it how well it worked.

sections.title: Scope and Scale of Deployments
sections.content:
The surveyed networks showed wide variation in size and scope. Deployments ranged from under 20 Label Switching Routers (LSRs) to over 1000 LSRs. Eight deployments used LDP in both edge and core networks, two on the edge only, and one in the core only. Most networks (over half) maintained more than one adjacency per session, with some having as many as four.

LDP had been deployed in the surveyed networks for varying lengths of time: three deployments under 1 year, two at 2 years, three at 3 years, and three for over 4 years. This range of experience levels strengthened the survey findings, showing stable long-term operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks ranged from small to enormous, and some had been using LDP for years without problems.

sections.title: What Networks Use LDP For
sections.content: Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs) were the primary driver for LDP deployment, cited by nine of the eleven respondents. Other applications included pseudowires (4 deployments, with 1 planned), Layer 2 VPNs (4), forwarding based on labels (2), and BGP-free core routing (1). Operators chose LDP over the alternative RSVP-TE protocol for various reasons: six did not need traffic engineering, five chose it for interoperability, five had vendor constraints, four cited ease of configuration, and three cited scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: Most networks used LDP to create private networks, like separate channels for different customers on shared infrastructure. They chose it because it was simple and their equipment supported it.

sections.title: Challenges Encountered
sections.content:
Operators reported three categories of issues: configuration problems (firewall filters blocking LDP sessions), vendor bugs (particularly in early versions, including traffic blackholing and unnecessary label withdrawals), and protocol-level problems. The main protocol issue was synchronization between LDP and the IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol). Slow IGP convergence delayed LDP convergence, and rapid IGP changes sometimes caused LDP to black-hole traffic until it caught up. Another reported issue was that silent failures in independent control mode did not propagate back to the head end of LSPs.

Overall, operators reported stable implementations and steady improvement over time. Most operational issues occurred in early versions of vendor implementations. The survey provides strong evidence that LDP had matured to the point where advancement was justified.
sections.plainLanguage: Early versions had bugs, and firewalls sometimes blocked the protocol. But after fixes, the protocol was stable. Keeping routing and label distribution in sync was the trickiest part.
